query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Toughness retention in equiatomic FCC high-entropy alloys is governed by the interplay between heterogeneous lattice strain–induced dislocation activity and the formation of nanoscale twin boundaries that together delay crack initiation and propagation. If these features are suppressed (e.g., via a heat treatment that reduces lattice strain heterogeneity), then the alloy’s toughness will diminish.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, equiatomic FCC high-entropy alloy displaying inherent heterogeneous lattice strain and a natural density of nano-twins at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled post-processing heat treatment (or adjust composition slightly) to reduce lattice strain heterogeneity and suppress the formation of nano-twin boundaries without changing the overall FCC structure.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted under quasi-static loading at room temperature to moderate elevated temperatures (up to about 800°C) where the alloy retains its FCC phase; deformation conditions should be similar between the baseline and treated samples.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale twin boundaries and complex dislocation structures (e.g., multiple kinks, jogs, and cross-slips) that stem from heterogeneous lattice strain.
generation.mechanism: In the as-processed HEA, localized lattice strain differences activate complex dislocation mechanisms and promote nano-twin formation. These features serve to absorb deformation energy and delay crack propagation, thereby retaining toughness. A reduction in strain heterogeneity (via heat treatment or compositional tuning) diminishes nano-twin density and alters dislocation behavior, which reduces the capacity of the alloy to accommodate plastic deformation and thereby leads to toughness loss.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated baseline, samples that undergo the heat-treatment (or similar intervention) will exhibit a measurable decrease in toughness (such as lower fracture resistance or reduced strain-to-failure) as detected by a reduction in nano-twin density and changes in dislocation structure.
generation.baseline: HEA samples in their initial processed state, maintaining their heterogeneous lattice strain, nano-twin network, and associated high toughness and ductility under standard mechanical testing conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for equiatomic or near-equiatomic FCC high-entropy alloys under quasi-static loading conditions at room to moderately elevated temperatures (up to approximately 800°C). Its validity for non-FCC structures or under very high strain-rate conditions remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative relationship between the degree of lattice strain heterogeneity, nano-twin density, and toughness retention is still not fully defined and may vary with processing history and minor compositional fluctuations. Further detailed microstructural studies are required to generalize the mechanism.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical FCC HEA samples. One set remains in the as-processed state (maintaining inherent heterogeneous lattice strain and nano-twinning), while the second set is subjected to a controlled heat treatment intended to reduce lattice strain heterogeneity and suppress nano-twin formation. Conduct mechanical tests (e.g., tensile tests and fracture toughness measurements) alongside microstructural characterization (via TEM and EBSD) to quantify nano-twin density and dislocation structures in both sets.
measurements: Nano-twin density and dislocation structure via TEM/EBSD
Comparison of microstructural features before and after intervention
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant decrease in nano-twin density and changed dislocation structures, or if these microstructural modifications are not accompanied by a corresponding reduction in toughness (e.g., similar fracture toughness and strain-to-failure as the baseline samples), then the hypothesis that heterogeneous lattice strain–induced twin formation governs toughness retention is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: From the images in Fig. 3, the nano-twins in the EBSD scans become very clear by overlaying the scan on an image quality, IQ, map of the same data set, which permits the measurement of the typical misorientation angle of 60° for twinning (Fig. 3e). We conclude from these results that between room and cryogenic temperatures where the strength, ductility and toughness of the medium-entropy CrCoNi are all simultaneously enhanced, nano-twinning contributes an important additional deformation mode that helps alleviate the deleterious effects of high strength that would normally be expected to result in lower toughness.

However, recent studies have shown that single-phase fcc high- and medium-entropy alloys (HEAs/MEAs) that are composed of three or more of elements Al, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, and Ni exhibit a rapid decrease in ductility at intermediate temperatures (400° to 800°C) (), as summarized in Fig. 1 and fig. S1. The common feature at stress-stain curves is that these alloys exhibit strain hardening and failure shortly after the maximum tensile stress is reached. Here, we reveal the fundamental mechanism for such a ductility loss and provide guidelines for avoiding this problem.

Our results reveal that the heterogeneous lattice strain causes unusual dislocation behaviors (i.e., multiple kinks/jogs and bidirectional cross slips), resulting in the strengthening mechanisms that underpin the strength-ductility synergy. The outcome of our research sheds important insights into the design of strong yet ductile distorted crystalline solids, such as high-entropy alloys and high-entropy ceramics.
